items.title: Big Tech Q3 2026 earnings — Alphabet beats on $127.6B revenue with 103% Cloud growth but shares fall ~8% on $51.4B capex and EPS miss; Meta beats revenue but EPS crushed by $9.89B litigation charge and tumbles after narrowing 2026 capex to $135–145B; hyperscaler 2026 capex total tracks around $700–725B
items.summary: Alphabet and Meta both reported Q3 2026 after the close on October 28 and October 29, and both beat revenue but got sold off hard on capex and bottom-line surprises. Alphabet posted $127.6B revenue (+25%) with Google Cloud up 103% YoY to $30.7B and Cloud operating margin expanding from 23.7% to 36.2% — but net income fell to ~$26.2B on equity-investment losses, Q3 capex hit $51.4B producing roughly negative $9.1B free cash flow, EPS of $2.12 missed consensus near $3.00, and shares dropped about 8% in after-hours trading. Meta reported $64.6B revenue versus $63.3B expected but GAAP EPS came in at $3.83 versus $6.67 expected, dragged by a $9.89B litigation charge; Q3 capex was $34.9B with negative FCF of about $2.12B, and the company narrowed 2026 capex guidance to $135–145B (from $130–145B) while guiding 'notably larger' AI investments in 2027. Combined with Microsoft and Amazon's prior guidance, the four hyperscalers are now tracking roughly $700–725B of calendar-2026 capex — up from a $410B total in 2025 and up from the ~$650B estimate circulating earlier in the year.
items.why_it_matters: This is the real test the market has been circling for weeks: whether the ~$800B of 2026 hyperscaler AI capex is actually translating into bottom-line discipline. The short answer from the Oct 28–29 prints is 'the top line is working, the bottom line isn't yet' — Alphabet's Cloud growth at 103% YoY is the biggest print in the quarter and vindicates the thesis that frontier-model demand is a durable top-line engine, while the stock reaction says investors are no longer willing to look through capex and EPS misses in the way they did in Q1 and Q2. For a hobbyist Python coder, the practical implication is twofold. First, API pricing: hyperscalers under capex pressure historically defend margin by raising enterprise pricing floors rather than consumer or developer-tier pricing, so the near-term risk to the $1/$5-per-million-tokens-type pricing you see on GPT-6.1 Terra and Mistral Large 4 is modest, but a rolling repricing of generous free tiers over 2027 is now more likely than it was last week. Second, model availability: Alphabet's 103% Cloud growth number includes Gemini API inference, which is a strong signal that Google is going to keep pushing API access to Gemini 4 (including whatever Carbon's public-API path becomes) rather than keeping it enterprise-only — Google needs the Cloud growth to keep printing. The $9.89B Meta litigation charge is a one-off reminder that these companies carry non-AI liabilities that can swamp a quarter — the $34.9B Meta Q3 capex is real, but the EPS reaction overstates how badly the AI business performed. The two things worth tracking into Q4 are (1) whether Microsoft's late-October print (fiscal Q1 2027, expected within days) also triggers a capex-reaction sell-off, and (2) whether Amazon's print after that extends the pattern — if three of four hyperscalers get punished for capex this cycle, the odds that one of them (likely Meta) trims the top end of its 2027 guide in January goes up. For the AI-coding workflow: nothing about today's prints changes which model is best for a given task; what might change over the next 6–12 months is which API endpoints are generously priced versus which get a 'frontier tier' pricing shelf stacked on top of them. The specific numbers to watch: Alphabet $190B 2026 capex guide for any revision, Meta's $135–145B range, and whether either changes 2027 guidance when they first set it in January.
items.why_it_matters_brief: Alphabet Cloud up 103% and Meta beats revenue, but both stocks sold off on capex and EPS misses — the market just stopped looking through hyperscaler AI spending the way it did two quarters ago.

items.title: OpenAI reportedly plans to buy Google TPUs — The Information scoop (Oct 27–28) says OpenAI is moving from renting to purchasing TPU capacity; Google has not confirmed, OpenAI has already posted TPU-tuning engineering jobs; Oracle reportedly plans to add TPUs to its cloud in 2027
items.summary: The Information reported on October 27, 2026 — and Reuters and multiple secondary outlets picked it up on Oct 27–28 — that OpenAI is preparing to purchase Google TPU chips rather than only renting TPU capacity through Google Cloud. OpenAI already began using rented Google TPU capacity in mid-2025; the reported shift to purchasing would be a direct supply-chain move. OpenAI declined to comment and Google has not confirmed. Supporting evidence: OpenAI has posted job listings for engineers to tune its models for TPU hardware. A separate thread of reporting (TrendForce) says Oracle is also planning to bring TPUs into its cloud offering in 2027, which would be the first time Google's TPU hardware is sold outside Google Cloud at scale. One Turkish-outlet report cites an earlier OpenAI spokesperson calling the company's TPU work 'early-stage testing with no plans for broad use,' so the Oct 27 report is a change from (or supersedes) that earlier framing. Volume, price, and timeline are not disclosed in the report. Alphabet reported Q3 earnings on Oct 28 (the day after the leak), and TPU demand was expected on the call — but Alphabet's prepared remarks and release did not call out an OpenAI-specific TPU deal, and no primary confirmation from either company has appeared as of this digest run.
items.why_it_matters: This is the clearest signal yet that the AI-chip buy-side is actively trying to diversify away from Nvidia's near-monopoly on frontier training and inference. OpenAI is Nvidia's single most prominent customer by brand — if the report is accurate and the purchase proceeds, it moves the narrative from 'everyone has to be on Nvidia' to 'the biggest Nvidia customer is quietly hedging.' For Gabe's Python stack specifically, the practical implications are a step removed but worth tracking: (1) PyTorch's XLA/TPU backend has been stable but second-class since the Google-TPU-via-Colab era — if OpenAI is tuning models for TPUs, the quality of the open-source Python toolchain for 'write PyTorch, run on TPU' goes up because that's exactly what OpenAI's engineers will have to improve to make their own work ship, which usually leaks back into open-source libraries like torch_xla and JAX; (2) if TPUs become a credible second supplier at the frontier, the per-token cost floor on inference goes down over 2027–2028 because the top labs can play Nvidia and Google against each other on compute pricing, and some of that will show up as cheaper API tokens; (3) the Oracle-TPUs-in-2027 angle, if real, is the one that matters for anyone who builds on top of multiple clouds, because it would be the first time a TPU-tuned model you could call from a non-Google cloud exists. Caveats worth carrying: the primary report rests on a single anonymous source per the Information, neither OpenAI nor Google has confirmed, and OpenAI's earlier public framing — 'early-stage testing, no broad use' — has not been formally retracted. The job-listings signal is real but not conclusive; companies tune for multiple hardware targets routinely. The specific numbers to watch over the next 4–8 weeks: (a) whether Google calls out a specific hyperscaler-tier customer by name in Q4 earnings or a Cloud Next announcement, (b) whether OpenAI publishes a benchmark or a technical post about TPU performance (that would be the clearest confirmation), (c) whether Oracle's rumored 2027 TPU rollout gets its own primary-source announcement from Oracle. The 'TPU is easier said than done' point from the TechRadar piece is also real — OpenAI's codebase is deeply tuned to CUDA, and 'swapping chips' involves rewriting training/inference stacks in ways that routinely take 6–18 months even for well-resourced teams.
items.why_it_matters_brief: If accurate, OpenAI buying rather than renting Google TPUs is the biggest signal yet that Nvidia's frontier-chip monopoly has a crack — and the Oracle-adds-TPUs-in-2027 side of the story is what makes it matter beyond one lab.

items.title: Mistral Large 4 open weights — afternoon update: first independent benchmarks land. Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0 scores Large 4 at 38 (vs 9 for Large 3), Vals ranks it 6th of 75 on the Harvey Legal Agent Benchmark at 15.83% behind Gemini 4 Argon's 19.58%, and independent evaluators measure the context window at ~524K tokens rather than Mistral's claimed 1M
items.summary: The Oct 30 am item noted Mistral Large 4's open-weight release on Oct 29 but flagged that independent benchmark comparisons against Gemini 4 Carbon and Opus 5.5 had not yet been published; through the afternoon of Oct 30, the first independent third-party benchmark results have started to appear. Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index v5.0 scores Mistral Large 4 at 38, a sharp step up from Large 3's score of 9 on the same index. For context, the current Index leaderboard places Gemini 4 Carbon at 59, Claude Opus 5.5 at 58, and GPT-6.1 Terra Astra at 57 — so Large 4 at 38 is a strong open-weight showing but materially behind the frontier closed models. On DeepLearning.AI's reporting of the Artificial Analysis per-task cost data, Mistral Large 4 at reasoning-mode scores 38 on the Intelligence Index at $1.13 per task, tying GPT-6 Luna's score (38) at a much higher per-task cost than Luna's $0.07. On Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark (via Vals), Mistral Large 4 ranks 6th of 75 at 15.83%, behind Gemini 4 Argon at 19.58%. Mistral's own-reported numbers remain unreproduced in the independent runs: DeepSWE 61.7% on agentic coding was evaluated privately before the harness went public, so it isn't externally verifiable. One data-point conflict surfaced in independent evaluation: Mistral's spec sheet lists a 1M-token context window, but independent evaluators report ~524K tokens of practical window — a 1.9x gap that is big enough to matter for long-context agent work. The HuggingFace listing and the 4× B200/B300 inference hardware requirement from the am remain accurate.
items.why_it_matters: This is the specific data Gabe needed to size up where Mistral Large 4 actually sits in the open-weight landscape, now that the first independent benchmarks have landed. The honest read: Large 4 is a credible open-weight contender that is clearly a step up from Large 3 on the same measurement framework (Artificial Analysis Index 38 vs 9), but it is not at the frontier of what the closed labs currently ship — Carbon (59), Opus 5.5 (58), and Terra Astra (57) all score 50%+ higher on the same composite. The useful framing for a hobbyist Python coder: Large 4 is 'the open-weight model that's good enough to run yourself when a frontier closed-API call isn't the right tradeoff,' not 'the open-weight model that replaces GPT or Claude for complex work.' Three practical consequences follow. First, the 524K vs 1M context-window discrepancy means that if Gabe is building anything that depends on actually using 1M tokens of context (long-codebase assistants, long-transcript summarization, long-document agents), Large 4 is probably not the right model to pin that workflow to — independent evaluators seeing ~524K means some of the attention past that point is degrading in ways that matter in practice. Second, the Vals Legal Agent 6th-of-75 finish at 15.83% is a reminder that even strong open-weight models still have specific-domain gaps compared to frontier closed models; for domain-specific agent work, the closed API that is cheapest-at-equivalent-quality is still often the right default, especially when the closed-model cost is in the $1-per-task range (GPT-6.1 Terra at $1/$5 per million). Third, the per-task cost structure: Artificial Analysis has Large 4 at $1.13 per Intelligence Index task, tying GPT-6 Luna's 38 at $0.07 per task — this is the metric that quantifies the cost of running the model yourself versus calling a cheap closed-API endpoint. For Gabe's actual week: the directional lesson from this update is that the open-weight landscape has a clearer price-performance frontier than it did 90 days ago, and the right place to spend any experimentation budget is probably at the top of that frontier (currently GPT-6 Luna or an equivalently cheap closed-API option) rather than at the self-hosted end, until you have a specific reason — license, latency, data-residency — to prefer self-hosting. The vLLM-and-SGLang Python inference path from the am still works and is still the right starting point for anyone who wants to try Large 4; nothing in the afternoon's benchmark reporting changes that. What has changed is a cleaner comparison baseline for the model's actual quality.
